verses.text: At the end of every seven years, you shall cancel debts.

This is the way it shall be done: every creditor shall release that which he has lent to his neighbor. He shall not require payment from his neighbor and his brother; because Yahweh’s release has been proclaimed.
Of a foreigner you may require it; but whatever of yours is with your brother, your hand shall release.
However there shall be no poor with you (for Yahweh will surely bless you in the land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance to possess it)
if only you diligently listen to Yahweh your God’s voice, to observe to do all this commandment which I command you today.
For Yahweh your God will bless you, as he promised you. You will lend to many nations, but you will not borrow. You will rule over many nations, but they will not rule over you.
If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother;
but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks.

Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your poor brother, and you give him nothing; and he cry to Yahweh against you, and it be sin to you.
You shall surely give, and your heart shall not be grieved when you give to him; because that for this thing Yahweh your God will bless you in all your work, and in all that you put your hand to.
For the poor will never cease out of the land. Therefore I command you to surely open your hand to your brother, to your needy, and to your poor, in your land.
If your brother, a Hebrew man, or a Hebrew woman, is sold to you, and serves you six years; then in the seventh year you shall let him go free from you.
When you let him go free from you, you shall not let him go empty.
You shall furnish him liberally out of your flock, out of your threshing floor, and out of your wine press. As Yahweh your God has blessed you, you shall give to him.
You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and Yahweh your God redeemed you. Therefore I command you this thing today.
It shall be, if he tells you, “I will not go out from you,” because he loves you and your house, because he is well with you;
then you shall take an awl, and thrust it through his ear to the door, and he shall be your servant forever. Also to your female servant you shall do likewise.
It shall not seem hard to you, when you let him go free from you; for he has been double value of a hired hand as he served you six years. Yahweh your God will bless you in all that you do.

You shall dedicate all the firstborn males that are born of your herd and of your flock to Yahweh your God. You shall do no work with the firstborn of your herd, nor shear the firstborn of your flock.
You shall eat it before Yahweh your God year by year in the place which Yahweh shall choose, you and your household.
If it has any defect, is lame or blind, or has any defect whatever, you shall not sacrifice it to Yahweh your God.
You shall eat it within your gates. The unclean and the clean shall eat it alike, as the gazelle, and as the deer.
Only you shall not eat its blood. You shall pour it out on the ground like water.

footnotes.content: Every seven years—a rhythm built into creation itself. God doesn't just forgive; He institutionalizes mercy, making it part of how His people live together. It's a radical idea: that debts, which chain us to the past, can be released and start fresh.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A creditor releases what he lent—not grudgingly, but because "Yahweh's release has been proclaimed." The Lord's freedom comes first; ours follows. When we let others off the hook, we're echoing what God does for us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A foreigner's debt can be collected, but your brother's is released. Not because outsiders matter less, but because kinship carries obligation. The covenant people belong to each other in a way that shapes how we handle money and trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "There shall be no poor with you"—a promise wrapped in condition. God sees poverty not as permanent but as something His blessing can lift. The dream is real; it depends on whether we listen and obey what comes next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The condition: listen to God's voice and keep His commandments. Prosperity isn't magic—it's the fruit of alignment. When we walk close to God's word, He opens His hand; when we drift, abundance slips away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You will lend to many nations, but you will not borrow." The image is clear: Israel lender, not debtor; ruler, not ruled. This describes a people anchored to God's covenant, standing in strength that flows from dependence on Him, not on foreign powers or alliances.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Do not harden your heart." The poor brother is right there—visible, known, at your gate. The first battle isn't about money; it's inside us. God watches whether we let compassion close or stay open when need appears.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not grudging help, but generous lending. "Sufficient for his need"—not excess or waste, but enough. The tone is generous abundance, a hand open wide, treating the poor as brothers, not problems.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beware the "base thought"—scheming to avoid giving because the release year approaches. God hears the cry of the refused poor. Stinginess born of calculation isn't prudence; it's sin, and it cuts you off from blessing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Give gladly, with a heart unburdened by regret. That lightness of spirit when you help—that's the mark of God's work in you. And the promise: He'll bless all you do, because your hands are learning His rhythm of generosity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The poor will never cease out of the land." A hard realism—we won't solve poverty by decree. But the command stands: keep your hand open. The work is endless because mercy is endlessly needed, and we're called to steady faithfulness, not utopian results.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A Hebrew servant works six years, then goes free in the seventh—a small sabbath for the servant's whole self. Even slavery in God's covenant carries dignity and an expiration date. No one is meant to belong to anyone but the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Release him empty and you've freed his body but not his future. Send him out with nothing and you've made freedom a cruel joke. God's release always comes with provision—it's the pattern we follow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Give liberally from what the Lord blessed you with—flock, threshing floor, wine press. The servant served faithfully; he leaves enriched, not stripped. This is how a covenant people treat those who've labored with them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Remember that you were a slave in Egypt, and Yahweh redeemed you." Memory anchors mercy. Your own bondage and rescue aren't ancient history—they're the living reason you treat the poor with open hands. This command flows from grace you've already received.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The servant says: I will not go free because I love you and your household and I'm well with you. Love and good treatment bind people more than law ever could. The best masters earn a servant's voluntary loyalty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The awl through the ear at the doorpost—a permanent mark, binding him forever. It's a striking image: the servant who chooses to stay does so visibly, before all. Covenant is written on the body, a sign of chosen belonging.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't begrudge letting a servant go—he's been worth double a hired hand over six years. Fair exchange, honest reckoning: he gave his labor, you give him his future and provision. The Lord will bless you for the generosity of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every firstborn male—flock and herd—belongs to the Lord. Not to be worked or sheared, but set apart. The first and best from the animals acknowledge that everything comes from God's hand and returns to His worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You eat the firstborn before the Lord in the place He chooses, year by year. Worship becomes a feast—the family gathers, the animal's life becomes a celebration of covenant. Holiness and joy aren't strangers; they feast together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A defective animal—lame, blind, any flaw—cannot be sacrificed. The Lord receives the unblemished best. It's not cruelty; it's respect, an ancient way of saying: what we offer to the Holy One must bear no stigma of our carelessness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A blemished firstborn you eat at home, clean and unclean alike. It feeds the family rather than the altar, but that, too, is provision. Not everything holy is for sacrifice; some abundance is for sustenance and sharing with those around your table.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo: do not eat the blood, pour it out like water. Across the centuries, this law reminds us that blood—life itself—belongs to God alone. We are receivers, stewards, not masters of the life poured out around us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
